title: Testing the Model
topic: Revising models with new data; Engage/Explore/Enrich structure

items.prompt: After building a math model, why is it important to test it against new data?

choices.A: Testing is never necessary once a model is built
choices.B: To check whether the model still makes accurate predictions, and revise it if needed
choices.C: To make the model more complicated

items.rationale: Good models are checked against real data and revised if they no longer fit.

choices.B: Three stages of a lesson: engage with the idea, explore it hands-on, then enrich with deeper practice

items.rationale: It's a three-part lesson structure moving from introduction to hands-on work to deeper practice.

items.prompt: A student's model predicted 20 classmates would prefer pizza, but a survey showed 26 actually preferred pizza. What should the student do?

choices.B: Revise the model so it better fits the real data
choices.D: Assume the survey must be wrong without checking

items.rationale: When a model doesn't match real data, mathematicians revise the model rather than dismiss the data.

items.prompt: A model predicted 20 students; the actual survey result was 26 students. What is the difference between the actual and predicted values?
Journaling about math work during Engage/Explore/Enrich time helps students most by:

choices.A: Providing a record of thinking and reasoning to revisit and revise
choices.B: Replacing the need to practice skills
choices.C: Counting only as a grade, with no other purpose

items.rationale: Journaling captures a student's reasoning so it can be reviewed and built on later.
